title: To the edge of the cliff (Luke 4:22–30)
hook: his own town loves him, then tries to throw him off a cliff, and he walks through them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nazareth manifesto, Isaiah's scroll and one word: today. Your line was today this is fulfilled. Did your one small thing happen before sundown? Day five hundred seventeen.

"Is not this Joseph's son?" It's said in the same synagogue, a minute after the reading, and at first it sounds proud. Luke says they "wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth." The hometown boy, all grown up. You can almost hear the aunties. But hometowns are complicated. The same people who love you also think they know exactly who you are, and exactly what you owe them. We've heard what you did in Capernaum, they're thinking. Do it here. Within a few verses, this warm room will become a crowd marching him to the edge of a hill.

Jesus names what they're thinking before they say it: "Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself." Then: "Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country." And he reaches for two stories from their own scriptures. In the days of Elijah there was a famine, and many widows in Israel. But the prophet was sent to a widow in Sarepta, in the region of Sidon, outside Israel. In the days of Elisha there were many lepers in Israel, "and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian." A foreign widow. A foreign general. Both from Israel's own prophets, both showing God's care reaching past the expected circle. That's the line that turns the room. Luke says "all they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath," and the scene moves fast: they "thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong." This isn't a story about one town being worse than others. It's about something any group can do: we love the prophet until the prophet says God's kindness isn't only ours. And then the ending, so quiet you can miss it: "But he passing through the midst of them went his way." No miracle is described. No fight, no speech, no running. He just walks through the crowd and keeps going. Luke doesn't explain how. The text is silent, and the silence is part of the picture: the anger doesn't get to decide his direction.
screen: `A WIDOW IN SIDON, A SYRIAN GENERAL.`
`FILLED WITH WRATH, TO THE BROW OF THE HILL.`
`THROUGH THE MIDST, AND ON HIS WAY.`
then, large: `HE PASSING THROUGH THE MIDST OF THEM WENT HIS WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay calm when praise turns. Settle, and breathe. Remember a time when people who liked you suddenly didn't: a group chat that went cold, a family dinner that soured, a boss whose praise flipped into blame. Notice whether it still shows up in your body: heat in the chest, the urge to argue or to win them back. Now picture Jesus at the edge of the hill, and the small, steady way he walks through. No shouting. No pleading. Breathe slowly, and let your shoulders drop. Imagine yourself doing the same: not fighting the crowd, not obeying it, just going your way. If you pray, you can ask for that steadiness. If you don't, simply practice the slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Patris, Greek for homeland, hometown: his own town wonders at him, then turns on him and takes him to a hilltop, and he walks through the middle of them and goes on.
Your line: he went his way. If praise turns to blame today, take one slow breath before answering, and keep walking in the direction you were already going. Day five hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Some Christians read the rejection at Nazareth as a picture of how hard it is to hear a prophet close to home, and Nazareth has a traditional hilltop site linked to the story.

fork.setup: your own town is pushing you toward the edge of a hill. what do you do?
options: give them the miracle they want.
pass through the middle of them and go your way.

fork.reveal: he walks through the crowd and keeps going. no fight and no explanation: the anger doesn't decide his direction.

original.note: Greek: homeland, home town. no prophet is accepted in his own patris.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mob that hated Jesus.
what it means: a hometown that loved him turns when he says God's care reaches past their circle, and he walks on through.
what a scholar hears: his examples, the widow of Sarepta and Naaman, come from 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 5, so his challenge is drawn from their own scriptures.
